edition.stripNote: Thu 19 Nov. Wednesday's session was the worst for commodities in weeks — a broad sell-off driven by hawkish FOMC minutes and a bearish API crude build. Gold plunged to a 52-week low of $3,722 per ounce, down 2.5%, marking its eighth consecutive decline — the longest losing streak in over a year. The FOMC minutes confirmed nearly all committee members judged an additional December rate hike to be appropriate, while Fed Governor Waller suggested a large hike might be needed, triggering the final hour of heavy selling. The dollar surged to a 19-month high of 103.84 and the 10-year Treasury yield held at 5.10%. Brent crude crashed 3.2% to $90.16 — its first close below $91 in two weeks — after the API reported a 5.28 million barrel crude inventory build, the largest in three months. WTI fell 2.2% to $84.08. Silver slid 3.3% to $45.22; platinum cratered 4.8% to $1,357; palladium fell 3.1% to $935. Newcastle coal held at $150, bucking the sell-off as winter demand and the Hormuz energy crisis sustained the thermal fuel bid. Copper extended losses from the DRC bridge collapse, falling a further 4.2% to $5.75 per pound ($12,675 per tonne LME) as the broader sell-off amplified supply-disruption fears. Base metals broadly weakened — zinc fell 4.1% to $3,529, tin slipped 2.5% to $45,500, while nickel bucked the trend with a 0.4% gain to $15,850 on Indonesian supply disruption fears. Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average to approximately $62,400, down 2.8%; Ethereum fell to $1,753; the Fear and Greed Index remains in Extreme Fear. Grains were hammered by the surging dollar — wheat plunged 25 cents to 570¢ per bushel, its lowest since January; corn fell 2.5% to 435½¢; soybeans eased 0.7% to 1,216¾¢. Cocoa fell 3% to $5,027 as ICE inventories hit a 2.5-year high of 3.8 million bags. Lithium was a rare bright spot, rebounding 3.2% to ¥91,800 per tonne. December rate-hike odds now sit at approximately 95%. Today brings two potentially transformative events: Anthropic begins trading on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT at a ~$1.4 trillion valuation, and the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit convenes in Shenzhen — the first-ever face-to-face meeting of all three leaders. The November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline is now 8 days away.

overview: Wednesday's commodity session was the worst in weeks — a broad sell-off driven by hawkish FOMC minutes and a bearish API crude inventory build. Gold plunged to a 52-week low of $3,722 per ounce, down 2.5%, marking its eighth consecutive decline as the FOMC minutes confirmed nearly all committee members favoured an additional December rate hike and Fed Governor Waller suggested a large increase might be needed. The dollar surged to a 19-month high of 103.84 and the 10-year Treasury yield held at 5.10%, creating a hostile environment for dollar-denominated commodities across the board. Brent crude crashed 3.2% to $90.16 — its first close below $91 in two weeks — after the API reported a 5.28 million barrel crude inventory build, the largest in three months; WTI fell 2.2% to $84.08. Silver slid 3.3% to $45.22; platinum cratered 4.8% to $1,357; palladium fell 3.1% to $935. Copper extended losses from the DRC bridge collapse, falling a further 4.2% to $5.75 per pound as the broader sell-off amplified supply disruption fears. Newcastle coal held at $150, bucking the commodity rout as winter demand and the Hormuz-driven LNG crisis sustained the thermal fuel bid. Grains were hammered by the surging dollar — wheat plunged 25 cents to 570 cents per bushel, its lowest since January; corn fell 2.5% to 435½ cents; soybeans eased 0.7%.

Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average to approximately $62,400, down 2.8%, while Ethereum fell to $1,753 — the worst weekly crypto plunge in months. The Fear and Greed Index remains in Extreme Fear. Anthropic's IPO was priced on November 18 at $70–$78 per share (~$1.4 trillion valuation), with trading under ticker ANT beginning today on the Nasdaq — the second-biggest IPO in history after SpaceX, and a further liquidity drain from risk assets. The Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit convenes in Shenzhen today — the first-ever face-to-face meeting of all three leaders — with Hormuz, nuclear arms, Ukraine and trade on the agenda. Experts expect no major deliverables but the optics could shift sentiment. The November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline is now 8 days away; the summit provides the last major diplomatic window. Base metals were broadly softer — zinc fell 4.1% to $3,529, tin slipped 2.5% to $45,500 — but nickel bucked the trend with a 0.4% gain to $15,850 as expectations of Indonesian RKAB supply disruptions resurfaced. Cocoa fell 3% to $5,027 as ICE warehouse inventories hit a 2.5-year high, capping upside despite persistent West African supply concerns. Lithium was a rare bright spot, rebounding 3.2% to ¥91,800 per tonne after slumping to a one-year low earlier this week. December rate-hike odds now sit at approximately 95%. Today's convergence of the Anthropic debut and the trilateral summit makes it one of the most event-dense days for markets in months.

watchItems.title: Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen today — Hormuz, critical minerals and nuclear arms on the agenda
watchItems.text: The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit convenes today (Thursday, November 19) in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting — the first-ever face-to-face meeting of all three leaders. The White House has listed nuclear arms reduction as an agenda item; Trump said he would raise Iran and Ukraine. Experts note Xi shares US interests in reopening the Strait of Hormuz and preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon. For commodity markets, the critical outcomes are whether the trilateral format produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework, any progress on critical mineral export controls ahead of the November 27 deadline (now 8 days away), and signals on broader trade policy. Monday's oil crash and Wednesday's further 3.2% decline in Brent suggest markets are repricing diplomatic probabilities. Experts expect no major deliverables — the optics and precedent matter more than concrete results — but any progress on Hormuz or critical minerals could trigger significant repricing across energy, helium, sulfur and strategic metals.

watchItems.title: Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq today under ANT — $1.4 trillion valuation, second-biggest IPO in history
watchItems.text: Anthropic begins trading on the Nasdaq today (Thursday, November 19) under ticker ANT, after pricing its IPO at $70–$78 per share on November 18. The offering of 825 million Class A shares implies a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion — the second-biggest IPO in history after SpaceX. Orders were approximately six times oversubscribed. A separate private placement sees seven chip-and-cloud suppliers — Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners — buying $26 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price. Analysts continue to cite the IPO as a factor draining liquidity from crypto and risk assets — Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average on Wednesday — and the first day of trading coincides with the trilateral summit, adding to what is already one of the most event-dense market days in months.

watchItems.title: FOMC minutes confirm broad hawkish consensus — December rate-hike odds surge to 95%, Waller suggests large hike
watchItems.text: The FOMC minutes released on Wednesday confirmed that nearly all committee members judged an additional rate hike in December to be appropriate, with the debate now centred on the size of the increase rather than whether to raise rates. Fed Governor Waller separately suggested a large December hike might be needed, triggering a final-hour sell-off across precious metals and risk assets. December rate-hike odds surged to approximately 95% for a 25-basis-point increase, with roughly 5% odds of a 50-basis-point move. Gold plunged to a 52-week low of $3,722 — its eighth consecutive decline. The dollar surged to a 19-month high of 103.84. The 10-year Treasury yield at 5.10% continues to make non-yielding assets like gold and crypto expensive to hold. The next FOMC meeting is December 8–9.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 8 days away — trilateral summit is the last window
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline for China's US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 8 days away. Today's trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium, 60–80% of germanium, and close to half of mined antimony. The suspension covers Article 2 of Beijing's December 2024 export-control order — the ban on dual-use shipments to US military end users remains in force. There is no public indication yet of what Beijing will do when the deadline arrives. Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. If the bans resume, Western semiconductor and defence supply chains face renewed disruption. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: 8th consecutive decline · 52-week low · down ~10% from Oct high · 10Y yield 5.10% · dollar 103.84 · Dec hike odds 95% · Waller hawkish
desk.sum: Gold futures plunged to $3,722 per ounce on Wednesday, down 2.5%, hitting a 52-week low and marking the eighth consecutive decline — the longest losing streak in over a year. The sell-off accelerated after FOMC minutes confirmed nearly all members favoured a December rate hike and Fed Governor Waller suggested a large increase might be needed. The dollar surged to a 19-month high of 103.84 and the 10-year Treasury yield held at 5.10%. December rate-hike odds climbed to approximately 95% for a 25-basis-point increase. Central bank buying remains structurally supportive but insufficient to offset the yield and dollar headwinds. Today's trilateral summit in Shenzhen and Anthropic's Nasdaq debut add further event risk.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Lowest since late 2025 · gold-silver ratio ~82 · down ~25% from Oct peak · FOMC sell-off amplified industrial demand concerns
desk.sum: Silver fell 3.3% to $45.22 per ounce on Wednesday, extending losses to the weakest level since late 2025 as the FOMC-driven sell-off hit precious metals and industrial commodities simultaneously. The gold-silver ratio holds near 82. Silver's dual precious-industrial profile makes it doubly vulnerable to rising yields and a strengthening dollar. With December rate-hike odds at 95% and the 10-year yield at 5.10%, the macro environment remains hostile. The break below $46 opens the next support zone around $43.50–$44.00. Today's trilateral summit could shift sentiment if it produces a Hormuz de-escalation framework.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $84.08 · first close below $91 in 2 weeks · API crude build 5.28M bbl · 3 US carriers in Gulf · trilateral summit today
desk.sum: Brent crude crashed 3.2% to $90.16 per barrel on Wednesday — its first close below $91 in two weeks — with WTI falling 2.2% to $84.08. The API reported a 5.28 million barrel crude inventory build, the largest in three months, compounding bearish pressure from the FOMC-driven sell-off. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf. Today's trilateral summit in Shenzhen is pivotal — a Hormuz ceasefire framework could send Brent towards $82–$85, while a disappointment could snap prices sharply higher as ceasefire pricing unwinds. The convergence of the summit and the Anthropic IPO makes today exceptionally volatile for energy markets.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$12,675/t · lowest since July · DRC bridge collapse + sell-off amplified losses · LME inventories up 11.5% in 2 weeks
desk.sum: Copper fell a further 4.2% to $5.75 per pound (approximately $12,675 per tonne LME) on Wednesday — the lowest since July — as the broader FOMC-driven sell-off amplified losses from the DRC bridge collapse. LME copper inventories have risen approximately 11.5% over the past two weeks. The dollar at a 19-month high of 103.84 makes dollar-denominated commodities expensive for non-US buyers. Emergency road assessments in the DRC continue, with alternative routes adding substantial time and cost. AI data-centre, EV and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers, but the hostile macro environment caps near-term upside.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~40% YTD · held steady despite commodity rout · LNG JKM ~$33 · winter demand approaching · trilateral summit today
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $150 per tonne on Wednesday, bucking the broader commodity sell-off as winter demand and the ongoing Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis sustained the thermal fuel bid. Coal is up approximately 40% year to date. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. December JKM activity reached a record high as Asian buyers scrambled for winter supply. Today's trilateral summit could be a turning point — a Hormuz ceasefire deal would begin to ease energy supply tightness and pressure coal prices, while failure would reinforce the substitution narrative through winter.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Cratered on FOMC sell-off · weakest in weeks · EV shift + rate headwinds · South African supply constrained
desk.sum: Platinum cratered 4.8% to $1,357 per ounce on Wednesday — the steepest daily decline in the precious metals complex — as hawkish FOMC minutes and Waller's remarks triggered heavy selling. The EV transition continues to pressure automotive catalyst demand. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. With the dollar at a 19-month high and December rate-hike odds at 95%, the macro environment is acutely hostile. Today's trilateral summit could shift sentiment if it produces a Hormuz de-escalation framework, easing energy costs for PGM-intensive hydrogen electrolysis projects.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Deep below $1,000 · down ~33% YoY · EV transition headwind dominant · weakest sustained level since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium fell 3.1% to $935 per ounce on Wednesday, extending further below the $1,000 level as the FOMC-driven sell-off hit the entire precious metals complex. This is the weakest sustained level since 2018. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains dominant. With the dollar at 103.84, yields at 5.10% and December rate-hike odds at 95%, the macro environment is acutely hostile. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support. Today's trilateral summit adds event risk but is unlikely to shift the structural EV headwind.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: Trilateral summit TODAY · 3 US carriers in Gulf · IRGC escalation continues · 135+ total incidents · Hormuz ceasefire framework on agenda
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz crisis remains at elevated levels as the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit convenes in Shenzhen today. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest concentration since 2003. Iran's IRGC continues to warn shipowners against using the American-backed southern route. The trilateral summit provides the most significant diplomatic window to date for a potential Hormuz ceasefire framework — the Atlantic Council notes Xi shares US interests in reopening the strait and lowering energy prices. Oil's 3.2% crash on Wednesday suggests markets are repricing diplomatic probabilities. A breakthrough could ease the energy supply crisis that has driven coal, helium and LNG prices to multi-year highs.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: 4½-month low · dollar at 19-month high crushing exports · WASDE tighter balance sheets · trilateral summit today
desk.sum: December corn settled at 435½ cents per bushel on Wednesday, down 2.5%, dropping to a four-and-a-half-month low as the surging dollar at a 19-month high crushed US export competitiveness. The FOMC-driven sell-off hit grains broadly. CBOT trends showed corn down sharply amid the dollar strength. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report provides a structural floor. Today's trilateral summit in Shenzhen could affect trade policy, including the Busan truce soybean commitments and broader grain flows. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Fell 25¢ · lowest since January · dollar crushing export competitiveness · SovEcon Russia estimate provides floor
desk.sum: December wheat plunged 25 cents to 570 cents per bushel on Wednesday — the lowest since January — as the surging dollar at a 19-month high hammered US grain export competitiveness. The decline was the steepest among major grains. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast — provides a structural floor, but dollar strength is currently the dominant force. Today's trilateral summit and APEC meeting could address the Abu Dhabi grain corridor, a potential bearish catalyst if stalled Black Sea shipments restart.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.17 · outperformed corn and wheat · trilateral summit today could address Busan soybean commitments
desk.sum: January soybeans settled at $12.17 per bushel (1,216¾ cents) on Wednesday, down 0.7%, outperforming corn and wheat as the soy complex proved relatively resilient in the broader grain sell-off. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates. Today's trilateral summit and the Trump–Xi bilateral could address the Busan truce soybean commitments, which require China to purchase at least 25 million tonnes per year through 2028. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor. The dollar at 103.84 remains a headwind.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,753 · broke 200-week MA · Fear & Greed Extreme Fear · weekly plunge ~12% · Anthropic ANT debuts today · $260B+ wiped this month
desk.sum: Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average on Wednesday, falling 2.8% to approximately $62,400 — its worst weekly plunge in months at approximately 12%. Ethereum dropped to $1,753. The Fear and Greed Index remains in Extreme Fear. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows continued, with IBIT and FBTC each falling approximately 2.2%. Anthropic begins trading today on the Nasdaq under ANT at a ~$1.4 trillion valuation, representing a continued liquidity drain from risk assets. The FOMC minutes confirmed hawkish consensus, with December rate-hike odds at 95%, adding macro headwinds. Key support levels: $60,000–$61,000 for Bitcoin, $1,700 for Ethereum.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$33 · TTF $29.50 · HH $3.25 · Dec JKM activity hit record high · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · trilateral summit today pivotal
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) has firmed to approximately $33 per MMBtu as December contract activity reached a record high ahead of peak winter demand, per S&P Global Platts. TTF sits near $29.50 per MMBtu; Henry Hub at $3.25. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. Today's trilateral summit is pivotal — a Hormuz ceasefire framework could begin the process of restoring Qatari LNG flows, while failure would reinforce the supply crisis through winter. Newcastle coal's resilience at $150 on Wednesday, despite the broader sell-off, underscores the thermal substitution dynamic.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · 3 carriers in Gulf · trilateral summit today · 8 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. Three US carrier strike groups in the Gulf continue to constrain Middle Eastern supply logistics. Today's trilateral summit could be a turning point — a Hormuz ceasefire deal would begin to ease the sulfur supply disruption, while failure would extend the crisis. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 8 days away. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC).

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · trilateral summit today · wheat plunge bearish for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Wednesday's grain sell-off — wheat plunging to its lowest since January — is modestly bearish for near-term fertiliser demand. Today's trilateral summit and APEC could affect trade policy and fertiliser flows. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 8 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · trilateral summit TODAY is last major window
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now 8 days away — when the suspension of China's US-specific export prohibition on antimony expires. Today's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. If addressed, Western supply chains could stabilise; if the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further. China produces close to half of global mined antimony.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 8 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · trilateral summit today · no public indication of Beijing's plans
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. Today's trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window before the November 27 deadline, now 8 days away. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60–80% of germanium. There is no public indication yet of what Beijing will do when the deadline arrives. The underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing.
desk.src: Fastmarkets · Startup Fortune · Rare Earth Exchanges

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Steady at $5.30 · upstream tightness in China and Europe · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. Today's trilateral summit could affect vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions are discussed alongside the November 27 deadline.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Sliding toward $5,000 · ICE inventories at 2.5-year high of 3.8M bags · West African supply concerns persist · El Niño risk
desk.sum: ICE cocoa fell 3% to approximately $5,027 per tonne on Wednesday as ICE warehouse inventories hit a 2.5-year high of 3,815,074 bags, capping upside despite persistent supply concerns from West Africa. Prices are sliding toward the psychologically important $5,000 level. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' remains a medium-term bullish factor. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high adds a headwind, but supply fundamentals continue to provide a floor.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: European cobalt prices under pressure on demand concerns · Rotterdam $17–18/lb · DRC bridge disruption affects logistics
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $35,000 per tonne, with European cobalt prices under pressure on demand concerns per Argus Media. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $17–18 per pound. The DRC bridge collapse, while primarily affecting copper routes, continues to have secondary effects on cobalt logistics from the same mining region. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift weighs on the structural demand outlook. Wednesday's broader commodity sell-off added macro headwinds to an already-weak market.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Rebounded 3.2% from one-year low · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · monthly change -10.8%
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate rebounded to ¥91,800 per tonne on Wednesday, up 3.2% from earlier this week's one-year low below ¥89,000. The rebound bucks the broader commodity sell-off. However, structural oversupply remains the dominant theme, with Goldman Sachs projecting a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. Lithium is still down approximately 10.8% over the past month. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Supply ramp-ups continue to outpace demand growth.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil crash reduces synthetic rubber costs slightly
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Wednesday's oil crash marginally reduced synthetic rubber production costs, slightly tilting the natural-synthetic balance. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The dollar at a 19-month high remains a headwind.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot steady ~$91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · AI data-centre demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide and has raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. Wednesday's market sell-off had limited impact on uranium, which trades on supply-demand fundamentals rather than financial sentiment.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Ex-China NdPr $109–121/kg FOB · Pr-Nd oxide rising on tighter supply · Nov 27 deadline 8 days · trilateral summit today
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide edged up to approximately $73 per kilogram domestically in China, with suppliers raising offers as futures strengthened and low-priced supply tightened per SMM. Ex-China prices sit at $109–121 per kilogram FOB, with CIF Rotterdam at $100–120 per kilogram. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony — now 8 days away — adds further uncertainty to the broader critical minerals complex. Today's trilateral summit provides a diplomatic window for critical mineral discussions.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · Benchmark Minerals

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption and Wednesday's broader commodity sell-off cap near-term gains.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Bucked sell-off on Indonesian supply disruption fears · RKAB quota tightening · shot up 2% intraday before reversing
desk.sum: LME nickel bucked the broader base metals sell-off on Wednesday, edging up 0.4% to $15,850 per tonne. Nickel initially shot up nearly 2% on heavy volume as expectations of Indonesian RKAB mining quota supply disruptions resurfaced, per SMM, before giving back most gains as the FOMC-driven sell-off hit. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB quotas continues to provide a floor. The global nickel surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Today's trilateral summit and APEC trade talks add uncertainty.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Declined on FOMC sell-off · LME backwardation still wide · cancelled warrants elevated · Myanmar ban constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin fell approximately 2.5% to $45,500 per tonne on Wednesday, dragged lower by the broader FOMC-driven base metals sell-off. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. However, macro pressure from the surging dollar and rising yields is currently overwhelming the supply-side support. The November 27 deadline adds geopolitical uncertainty to the broader metals complex.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: Lowest since late July · 4-day losing streak · Chinese smelter restarts adding supply · TCs deeply negative · smelter curtailments continue elsewhere
desk.sum: LME zinc fell 4.1% to $3,529 per tonne on Wednesday — the lowest since late July — extending a four-day losing streak as Chinese smelter restarts after maintenance added supply pressure. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments outside China. The dollar at a 19-month high and FOMC-driven sell-off compounded the decline. The structural supply deficit remains intact, but the hostile macro environment caps near-term upside. Zinc is still up approximately 18% year-over-year despite recent weakness.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 8 days to Nov 27 deadline · trilateral summit today
desk.sum: European tungsten APT holds at $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu — Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 8 days away. Today's trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin format raises hopes for a broader deal that could include tungsten alongside gallium, germanium and antimony. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · trilateral summit today pivotal · IRGC escalation continues
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Today's trilateral summit could be pivotal for helium if it produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework — Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium, and any path to restoring Ras Laffan operations would need Hormuz de-escalation first. Russia's export controls extend through 2027.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · wheat plunge bearish for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Wednesday's grain sell-off — wheat plunging to its lowest since January — is modestly bearish for near-term fertiliser demand. The ongoing Hormuz crisis further reduces the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising, keeping the cost structure elevated.

quiz: Gold fell to a 52-week low of $3,722 per ounce on Wednesday, marking its eighth consecutive daily decline, after FOMC minutes confirmed nearly all members favoured a December rate hike.
Brent crude rallied 2% to $95 per barrel on Wednesday after the API reported a 3 million barrel draw in US crude inventories, easing oversupply concerns.
Brent actually crashed 3.2% to $90.16 — its first close below $91 in two weeks. The API reported a 5.28 million barrel crude inventory BUILD (not a draw), the largest in three months.
December wheat fell 25 cents to 570 cents per bushel on Wednesday, hitting its lowest level since January, as dollar strength weighed on US grain exports.
Bitcoin surged above $70,000 on Wednesday as the FOMC minutes revealed dovish dissent, with three governors voting for a rate pause ahead of the December meeting.

Bitcoin actually fell 2.8% to approximately $62,400, breaking below its 200-week moving average. The FOMC minutes confirmed hawkish consensus — nearly all members favoured a December hike — and December rate-hike odds surged to 95%.
Copper fell approximately 4.2% to $5.75 per pound on Wednesday — its lowest since July — extending losses from the DRC bridge collapse as the broader FOMC-driven sell-off intensified.
LME nickel plunged 5% on Wednesday as Indonesian RKAB mining quota expansions were confirmed, adding new supply to an already-oversupplied market.

Nickel actually bucked the sell-off, edging up 0.4% to $15,850, initially rallying nearly 2% on expectations of Indonesian supply disruptions from potential RKAB quota TIGHTENING (not expansion) before giving back most gains.
Anthropic's IPO was priced at $70–$78 per share on November 18 at a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion, with trading under ticker ANT beginning on the Nasdaq on November 19.
Chinese lithium carbonate futures fell to a fresh one-year low of ¥85,000 per tonne on Wednesday as Goldman Sachs raised its global surplus estimate to 600,000 tonnes by 2028.

Lithium actually rebounded 3.2% to ¥91,800 per tonne — a rare bright spot in the broader sell-off. It had already hit its one-year low earlier in the week. Goldman's surplus estimate remains at 444,000 tonnes, not 600,000.
